title: Sparkling Wine
description: Where the bubbles come from, and how each method gives a different wine.
L: Explain where the bubbles come from
Name the main methods of making sparkling wine

Most sparkling wines start as a dry, still base wine. Yeast and sugar are added, and a second fermentation takes place in a sealed vessel, a bottle or a pressurised tank. The carbon dioxide can't escape, so it dissolves in the wine. Champagne reaches about 6 atmospheres; Prosecco and other lighter styles often less.
Second fermentation in a closed vessel

The traditional method makes the second fermentation in the bottle you buy. The transfer method ferments in bottle, then empties the wine into a tank to filter it. The tank method ferments in large pressurised tanks. The cheapest way is carbonation, injecting gas like soda, which gives large, short-lived bubbles.
Match each method to how it works.
Each method traps carbon dioxide in a different way.

Fermenting in bottle leaves the wine in contact with dead yeast, the lees, for months or years. That adds bread, brioche and biscuit flavours and finer bubbles. Tank fermentation is fast, often weeks, and keeps fresh, fruity, floral aromas. Neither is better: they suit different grapes and styles.
All sparkling wines get their bubbles from a second fermentation.
Not true. The cheapest are carbonated, with gas injected directly. Their bubbles are coarser and fade faster.
Bubbles come from carbon dioxide trapped during a second fermentation
Traditional, transfer, tank and carbonation are the main methods
Bottle fermentation adds toasty notes; tank keeps fresh fruit
Put the steps of the traditional method in order

A dry base wine is blended, then bottled with sugar and yeast, the liqueur de tirage. The bottle is sealed with a crown cap. A second fermentation raises alcohol by about 1.2 to 1.5% and makes carbon dioxide. The wine then rests on its lees, from 15 months for non-vintage Champagne to many years for top wines.
Tirage, second fermentation, ageing on lees

Riddling, or remuage, slowly turns and tilts the bottles until the dead yeast slides into the neck. It once took weeks by hand; machines called gyropalettes now do it in about a week. The neck is frozen and the cap removed: pressure pushes out the plug of ice and yeast. This is disgorgement. Then sweetened wine, the dosage, is added.
Put the steps of the traditional method in order.
Add sugar and yeast, and seal
The order ensures the yeast does its work, adds flavour, and is then removed cleanly.

Dosage is a mix of wine and sugar added after disgorgement. It balances the high acidity of the base wine and decides the final sweetness: most Champagne is Brut, with up to 12 g/l. Brut Nature has none added. The traditional method is used for Champagne, Cava, Crémant, Franciacorta and many others.
Removing the frozen plug of yeast from the neck
Disgorgement removes the yeast sediment, using the wine's own pressure to push out a frozen plug.
The second fermentation happens in the bottle you buy
Riddling moves the yeast to the neck; disgorgement removes it
Dosage balances acidity and sets the sweetness
Explain how the tank method works
Explain why it suits aromatic grapes
Compare it with the traditional method

In the tank method, also called Charmat or Martinotti, the base wine goes into a sealed, pressurised tank with sugar and yeast. The second fermentation takes days or weeks. The wine is then filtered under pressure and bottled. The whole process can take as little as a month.
Second fermentation in a pressurised tank

Glera, Muscat and similar grapes have delicate floral and fruit aromas. Long contact with yeast would cover them with bready notes. The tank method keeps them fresh. It is also cheaper and faster, so the wines are affordable, made to drink young, and usually show larger, softer bubbles than Champagne.
Tank: fresh fruit, made to drink young
Which wine is typically made by the tank method?
Prosecco is made by the tank method. Champagne, Cava and Franciacorta use the traditional method.
Keep tank-method wines in a cool place and drink them within a year or two. Their charm is freshness, and it doesn't last.
What are typical features of tank-method sparkling wine?
Bread and biscuit notes come from long ageing on lees in bottle, typical of the traditional method.
The tank method ferments in sealed tanks, often in weeks
It preserves fresh fruit and floral aromas
It's faster and cheaper, and the wines are best young
Describe the Champagne region and its grapes

Champagne lies about 150 km north-east of Paris, one of the coolest wine regions in France. Grapes ripen barely, giving very high acidity, perfect for sparkling wine. The main grapes are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. Most Champagne is a blend of several years, called non-vintage, to keep a consistent house style.
Cool climate, high acidity, three grapes

Champagne's chalk soils drain well yet hold water deep, and the chalk cellars dug beneath Reims and Épernay stay at about 10 to 12 degrees all year, ideal for long ageing on lees. Non-vintage must age at least 15 months, vintage at least 3 years. That ageing gives the toasty, brioche notes.
The three main grapes of Champagne are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot ____.
Pinot Meunier, often just Meunier, is the third main grape, giving fruit and roundness.

Cava, mostly from Catalonia, uses local grapes like Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada, with 9 months minimum on lees. Crémant is made in eight French regions, like Alsace, Burgundy and the Loire. Franciacorta, in Lombardy, uses Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. England's south, on chalk like Champagne's, is a rising star.
Match each sparkling wine to its origin.
All of these use the traditional method, with different grapes and rules.
Champagne is cool and chalky, with three main grapes
Non-vintage ages at least 15 months on lees; vintage at least 3 years
Cava, Crémant, Franciacorta and English sparkling use the same method
Explain how Asti keeps its sweetness

Prosecco comes from north-east Italy, in the Veneto and Friuli. It must be at least 85% Glera. Most is made by the tank method, giving pear, apple and white flower aromas, light body and fresh acidity. The top area is Conegliano Valdobbiadene, a DOCG of steep hills, with the single slope of Cartizze at its peak.
Glera, tank method, pear and flowers

Asti and Moscato d'Asti come from Piedmont and are made from Moscato Bianco. Instead of a second fermentation, the juice is chilled and stored, then fermented once in a sealed tank. Fermentation is stopped by cooling and filtering, leaving sugar and only 5 to 7% alcohol. Asti is fully sparkling; Moscato d'Asti is gently fizzy, frizzante.
Asti is made with a second fermentation, like Prosecco.
Not true. Asti uses a single fermentation in a sealed tank, stopped early to keep sugar and low alcohol.

Both are made to drink young and well chilled. Prosecco suits aperitifs and light dishes; Extra Dry is the most common style, slightly sweeter than Brut. Moscato d'Asti, sweet and low in alcohol, suits fruit desserts and, in Piedmont, sometimes breakfast pastries.
Which grape is the main grape of Prosecco?
Prosecco must be at least 85% Glera. Moscato Bianco is the grape of Asti.
Prosecco is mostly Glera, made by the tank method
Asti and Moscato d'Asti come from one fermentation, stopped early
Both are best young and chilled
Compare the traditional and tank methods
Put these traditional method steps in order.
Yeast first does its work, then is moved and removed, and the wine is topped up.
Match each wine to its method.
Method shapes flavour, bubble and price.
What gives traditional method wines their bready, toasty notes?
Long contact with dead yeast in the bottle releases those flavours.
Which are traditional method sparkling wines?
Prosecco is mostly made by the tank method.
Moscato d'Asti is fermented to dryness and then sweetened.
Not true. Its fermentation is stopped early, leaving natural sugar and low alcohol.
Bubbles come from a second fermentation in a closed vessel
The traditional method gives toasty, fine bubbles; tank keeps fruit fresh
Champagne, Cava, Crémant and Franciacorta use the traditional method
Prosecco uses the tank method; Asti a single, stopped fermentation
